_comment: Compatibility data for the Build yours configurator. microduck/recipe.py and site/build.js both evaluate this file with the same small algorithm; neither holds a combination of its own. 'support' is the single table that says which locomotion each controller supports and through which drive. 'why_not' explains unsupported rows. 'rules' add recipe content, or block a selection with a reason and a nearest change. The default camera is not written here: microduck/recipe.py reads it from config/assembly.json (camera.preset). 'manifest_map' and 'report_controller' give the names stl/manifest.json and reports/assembly.json use for a controller or head. Row status: 'report' (read from reports/assembly.json and reports/sim.json for the selected controller, camera and head), 'defined' (defined, not designed), 'summary' (read from the variants summary when it exists, otherwise being analysed). Currents are whole mA in multiples of 10.
not_built: Nothing on this page has been physically built. No part has been printed against a servo or a motor, no robot has been assembled or powered.
trademarks: LEGO, Mindstorms and Technic are trademarks of the LEGO Group, which does not sponsor, authorise or endorse this project. Raspberry Pi is a trademark of Raspberry Pi Ltd. Arduino, UNO Q, TinkerKit and Braccio are trademarks of Arduino. No affiliation with any of them.

why_not.reason: The biped has six position joints. The EV3 brick has four output ports, the Build HAT four connectors and the BaseX four motor ports; the 51515 hub has six ports, but no six-motor leg has been drawn. The owner's LEGO prototypes use two motors and cranks instead: that is the crank walker.
Continuous-rotation servos and DC gear motors hold no angle, so they cannot be the biped's leg joints. They are offered as wheel drives.
The crank walker needs continuous rotation at each side's gear axle. The Braccio servos turn 180 degrees (published).
The crank walker's two sides must be phased from encoder positions (the prototype README says so). These drives have no position feedback, and no coupling to the Technic gear axle has been drawn.
The Braccio servos turn 180 degrees (published); they cannot drive a wheel round.
The EV3 brick cannot drive hobby servos: its four output ports drive LEGO motors (the Linux drivers list tacho-motor, dc-motor and led modes only).
The 51515 hub cannot drive hobby servos: its six ports are LEGO Power Functions 2.0 ports for LEGO motors and sensors.
A bare DC motor on an H-bridge board has nowhere to connect on a LEGO controller.
51515 motors have LEGO Power Functions 2.0 plugs; the EV3 brick's ports take EV3 and NXT plugs.
EV3 motors have EV3 plugs; the hub's ports are LEGO Power Functions 2.0. No adapter is documented by LEGO.
The Build HAT fits Raspberry Pi computers with a 40-pin GPIO header (Raspberry Pi documentation).
The BaseX is a base for an M5Stack Core and talks to it over the Core's I2C bus (M5Stack documentation).
This drive means motors plugged into the 51515 hub's own ports; this controller has no such ports.
This drive means motors plugged into the EV3 brick's own ports; this controller has no such ports. On an M5Stack Core the EV3 motors go on the BaseX.
The Braccio shield is an Arduino UNO format shield. No fit to this controller is documented.
On the UNO Q the six servos go through the Braccio shield, which is what was analysed. A separate I2C servo driver on the UNO Q has not been checked.
The BaseX has two servo outputs (M5Stack documentation): two for six joints. Hobby servo or DC motor drives on an M5Stack Core are not among the bases defined here.
Only the biped's deck has a variant for a full-size Raspberry Pi. The crank walker prototype and the wheeled variants are drawn around the Pi Zero 2 W.
The crank walker is defined only with LEGO motors: on a Raspberry Pi through the Build HAT, on the EV3 brick, on the 51515 hub, or on an M5Stack Core through the BaseX.

set.mechanism: Six-servo biped: left and right hip roll, hip pitch and knee pitch, one hobby servo per joint. No yaw, no ankles, no head: the torso carries a camera mount at the front edge of the deck. Four SR431 at the hips, two SR311 at the knees.

parts.note: hip roll and hip pitch

parts.name: SR311 servo (TinkerKit Braccio kit)
parts.note: knees

parts.name: Servo horn with centre screw (from the kit)
parts.note: also the drilling jig for the printed blanks

parts.name: Small cable tie
parts.note: two per servo. Each cradle has four tie slot pairs; the assembly test found at least two tie paths per cradle clear of the shaft and horn, on the assumed shaft position

parts.name: Horn screws for the printed blanks
parts.note: at least two opposed per horn; size to suit the horn, not specified by the design

assembly: Print the fit pieces at 100 percent scale. Try a servo of each size between the rails, both tie paths, the horn on the drill blank, and the camera board in its fit piece.
Read the assembly findings on the biped page before printing the set.
Print one of each of the other files. Use the horn as a drilling jig on each circular blank.
Centre each servo with the horns off. Strap two SR431 to the torso for hip roll, fit each yoke to its horn with the second SR431 facing outward for hip pitch.
Fit each thigh at its circular end, strap an SR311 at the far end for the knee, and fit the shin to the knee horn, toes forward.
Dry-assemble one leg and sweep it by hand, unpowered, before building the second.

wiring: No camera: the mount at the front of the deck stays empty. The torso listed is the one for the default camera preset.

The camera board stands in the mount at the front edge of the deck, lower edge on the corner seats, back against the ledges, held by the snap lips, lens the way the toes point and 10 degrees below level. Each board has its own torso file and fit piece.
assembly: Print the camera fit piece before the torso and try the board in it: 0.5 mm is allowed each side and 0.3 mm under the lips.

rules.block: The biped's torso is generated with a mount for one of three boards: the ESP32-CAM, the ESP-EYE or the ESP32-S3-EYE. No torso exists for this camera. Plates for a Pixy and its pan-tilt base exist as parts (head_pixy_plate_pixy2.stl, head_pixy_plate_pixy1.stl) but they are not placed on the biped: no torso carries one and no check includes one.

assembly: Print fit_lego_compatible_coupon.stl flat, studs up, and try a pin and a brick on each marked pair before printing the robot; the generator's HOLE_EXTRA and STUD_UNDER set the allowance.

rules.reason: The committed parts carry the pin holes and studs. Parts without them are not in the repository: they mean running the design's generator with its LEGO switches (torso, thigh, shin, foot) off, and that set was not analysed.

analysis: Not analysed: the parts regenerated without pin holes and studs.

set.mechanism: Two-motor parallel-crank walker from the owner's LEGO prototypes: one motor per side turns two cranks through three 16-tooth gears, and each leg hangs from the two crank tips. Crank radius 12 mm, 24 mm of fore-aft foot travel. Two driven axes, not six joints.

parts.name: Technic cross axle
parts.note: three per side through the chassis panel; lengths not fit-tested

parts.name: Technic bushes, pins and liftarms
parts.note: to retain the axles, pivot the legs and hold the motors; layout and quantities not fit-tested

assembly: Print the coupon, broad face down. Try a cross axle in the keyed hole, a pin in the 4.95 mm hole and a turning axle in the 5.35 mm bearing; the axle must spin freely.
Print one gear and one crank and check them on an axle before printing the rest.
Pass three cross axles through each side panel. Fit a gear to each inside the panel, in one plane; the centre gear idles. Fit a crank to each outer axle outside the panel, both at the same angle.
Pin each leg's two upper holes to the two crank tips, soles inward, the opposite leg half a turn out of phase.
Couple one motor to each side's rear gear axle and hold its housing at two points with Technic beams.
With the motors unplugged, turn each side by hand through a full revolution. Then, body supported, jog one port at a time. Set the phase from the encoder positions before running both sides.

parts.note: required: the controller's pins cannot drive a motor directly

parts.note: voltage and current not verified; separate from the controller's supply, grounds joined

wiring: Pins the driver needs from the controller. TB6612FNG: AIN1, AIN2, PWMA, BIN1, BIN2, PWMB and STBY (seven; five if STBY is tied high and both PWM pins are kept). DRV8833: AIN1, AIN2, BIN1, BIN2 with PWM on the inputs (four), nSLEEP high. L298N: IN1 to IN4 plus ENA and ENB (six). At least two of the pins must be PWM capable.
Pin names follow the chip makers' datasheets and were not re-read for this page. Which controller pins to use is not defined.
Speed is open loop: without the encoder version of the motor the controller cannot tell how fast a wheel turns, so the robot will not hold a straight line by itself.

parts.name: M5Stack 360 degree servo for head pan
parts.note: LEGO-compatible bracket on the Servo Kit 360 version (published); same SG90 case assumed. The BALA-C supplies two; whether they are the same part is not verified.

wiring: This servo turns continuously: the pulse sets speed and direction, not angle (M5Stack). It cannot hold or return to a head angle by itself; it would run the platform into a printed stop. A positional SG90-class servo is the safer choice.
Restrict the pan travel mechanically and leave cable slack.

Head servo signal: a spare channel of the servo driver board.
Head servo signal: a Pi GPIO pin with PWM. Under a Build HAT that needs the optional tall header (Raspberry Pi); which pins the HAT leaves free is not verified.
Head servo signal: one of the BaseX's two servo outputs (published).
The wheels already use two of these servos. A BALA-C supplies two in all, so the head needs a third.
